chapters.desert: Chapter 1 'Red Sand Silk Road' (赤沙古道): a Silk Road oasis city swallowed by quicksand, where Ba the drought goddess (旱魃) has awoken and turned the city's people, beasts and statues into sand fiends. Chinese mythology (Shan Hai Jing) and Dunhuang cave art. Palette: ochre-red sandstone, faded Dunhuang mural colours (malachite green, cinnabar red, lapis blue), old gold; the corrupting fire is a blazing white-gold sun fire with heat shimmer.
chapters.frost: Chapter 2 'Kunlun Snow Ruins' (昆仑雪墟): the 'lower capital of the Heavenly Emperor' on Mount Kunlun from the Shan Hai Jing, a mountain city of white jade terraces, verdigris bronze ritual gates, frozen waterfalls and the frozen Jade Pool of the Queen Mother of the West. Zhuyin the Torch Dragon (烛阴) has closed its eyes and the mountain sank into an endless polar night; its beasts, guardians and pilgrims froze into frost fiends. Palette: glacier blue, moon white, pale jade green and verdigris bronze, with a little faded vermilion; the corrupting power is a cold cyan-violet aurora frost fire (polar-night ghost light) glowing from cracks and crystals.
chapters.frost_b: Chapter 2, alternative direction 'Cold Mountain Taoist Abbey' (寒山道观): a Taoist immortals' abbey hanging on snowy cliffs in the style of the Hanging Temple, all timber halls on stilts, red-lacquered posts, grey tiled roofs heaped with snow, bronze alchemy furnaces and paper talismans. Yuqiang (禺强), god of the North Sea and the north wind, blew an eternal winter through it; its disciples, puppets, flying swords and guardian beasts froze into frost fiends. Palette: dark weathered timber, cinnabar-red lacquer, slate-grey tiles, yellow talisman paper and snow white; the corrupting power is a pale jade-green cold ghost fire (寒毒) seeping from talismans and furnace mouths.
chapters.frost_c: Chapter 2, alternative direction 'North Sea of Ice' (北冥冰海), from the opening of the Zhuangzi: 'In the northern darkness there is a fish named Kun; it changes into a bird named Peng'. A frozen polar sea at the end of the world: ancient wooden junks locked in the sea ice, whale-bone arches and cairns on the shore, glacier cliffs and ice caves, nomad felt tents. The great Kun stirs beneath the ice and the whole sea has frozen around it; its creatures and the drowned sailors froze into frost fiends. Palette: deep night-sea teal and ink blue, glacier white, weathered bone ivory and old ship-timber brown; the corrupting power is a cold bioluminescent aqua-cyan deep-sea glow.
chapters.frost_d: Chapter 2, alternative direction 'Beiting Ice Legion' (北庭冰甲营): a Tang-dynasty frontier garrison of the Beiting Protectorate that held a snowbound mountain pass against an endless winter and froze at its post. Its soldiers march on as an undead ice legion in frost-crusted Tang lamellar armour, iron face masks and red-tasselled helmets, with war drums, banners, crossbows, hand cannons and armoured war beasts. Palette: deep Tang lacquer red and dark iron, aged bronze, white fur trims and snow, against a bright cold cyan ice glow from eye slits, armour cracks and weapon edges.
chapters.inferno: Chapter 3 'Zhurong's Fire Prison' (祝融火狱): the underground forge-palace and prison of Zhurong (祝融), the fire god of Chinese myth, deep under a volcano: black basalt pillars, black-iron halls, giant bronze ding cauldrons and furnaces, hanging chains, fire altars and rivers of lava. The god's fire has run wild and turned his smiths, jailers, forge-made constructs and fire beasts into fire fiends. Palette: black iron and basalt black, molten lava orange and vermilion lacquer red, with dark bronze; the corrupting fire is a deep molten lava-orange glow with yellow-hot cores, glowing from cracks, seams, mouths and vents (never the white-gold sun fire of chapter 1).
chapters.plateau: Chapter 4 'Snowland Sky Road' (雪域天路): the high grassland plateau of western Sichuan and eastern Tibet, a wide green summer meadow basin ringed by snow peaks and a glacier, with a turquoise holy lake, a glacial river, stone watchtowers and colourful prayer flags. In myth the Yellow Emperor flayed Kui (夔), the one-legged thunder beast, to make a war drum; Kui's thunder soul slept in the holy lake and has now woken: thunderstorms sweep the plateau, and its marmots, yaks and the strange beasts of the Shan Hai Jing's Western Mountains are charged with corrupted thunder. Creature palette: plateau animal colours (greyish brown, cream white, rusty red, soot black) with weathered copper and bone accents; the corrupting thunder is a magenta-violet lightning glow with white-hot cores, showing as glowing zig-zag veins, crackling fur tips, glowing eyes and the weak spot (never the white-gold sun fire of chapter 1, the cyan-violet frost of chapter 2 or the lava orange of chapter 3). No people, no religious figures or symbols.

Wears scraps of old Chinese lamellar armour (a small chest plate and one shoulder plate), a ragged crimson neck scarf, and a small bronze bell glowing white-gold fixed between its ears (weak spot). Small hands with a clearly separate thumb and four separate fingers. Mischievous, twitchy, cute but dangerous.

designs.name: 饕餮
designs.brief: Taotie (饕餮), the insatiable glutton of Chinese myth whose face is the 兽面纹 / taotie motif cast on Shang and Western Zhou ritual bronzes (like the Houmuwu ding and the bronze gong vessels), and the Shan Hai Jing glutton with 'eyes under its armpits, tiger teeth and human-like claws'. A squat, massive, low beast about 5 m tall at the shoulder, built like a living Shang bronze vessel: NO fur at all; the whole body is cast bronze with thick verdigris-green and dark brown patina, worn golden highlights on the raised edges, every surface filled with fine low-relief squared cloud-and-thunder spirals (云雷纹). Its HEAD is the classic taotie mask, perfectly symmetric and as wide as its chest: a raised vertical flange ridge (扉棱) down the middle of the face, two huge bulging round eyes with pupils set in long almond eye sockets with hooked corners (臣-shaped), big C-shaped horns curling outward like the motif's horns, flat curling brows and ears, and a wide lower jaw hanging open with tiger fangs, sculpted lake water pouring into it as it swallows a lake. Its body is short and barrel-like, the belly a deep bronze cauldron (鼎) shape with ridged flanges along the spine; four thick column legs like the legs of a square ding, ending in clawed human-like hands. Its real eyes: two glowing magenta-violet eyes set in the armpits, under the front legs, clearly visible in the main pose where it rears up with one foreleg raised (weak spots). Thin magenta lightning glows in the cracks of the patina. Distinctly ancient CHINESE Shang dynasty bronze, NOT an Aztec, Mayan or Mesoamerican stone mask, not a furry bear or yak, not a realistic person.

The FRONT, SIDE and BACK views and the main pose must all show the same four legs (in the side view both near legs are clearly visible, front and hind).
